clue.text: Carpet stand fringing big town ground overlooking wicket

indicators.note: the word for stand is placed around the edges of the rest, as a fringe borders a carpet

parts.note: to stand something is to brook or tolerate it

indicators.note: ground is a past participle meaning crushed and broken up, so these letters are reworked
overlooking means ignoring or leaving out, so the wicket letter is dropped from big town

parts.note: W is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for wicket

explanation.surface: A rug-seller's display stand bordered with a city map, laid on a cricket ground beside the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpet' is a verb here, to reprimand, not a rug. 'overlooking' leaves BIGTON, which 'ground' turns into INGTOB.
explanation.definitionFit: To carpet someone is to haul them up for a telling-off, which is exactly calling them to account.

clue.text: Gallery is beginning to employ lift

parts.note: RA is the Royal Academy, a London art gallery and institution
taken as written

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, here of employ

explanation.surface: An art gallery starts taking on staff to boost its profile.
explanation.definitionFit: To lift something is to elevate or hoist it, a plain synonym of the verb.

clue.text: I'm near overturned drink? Tiresome thing on reflection

definitions.note: a whole statement standing for a person who might say it of themselves; near means stingy

indicators.note: in a down light, overturned means the word for drink is turned upside down, reading backwards

parts.note: gin is a spirit, a drink

indicators.note: a reflection shows things back to front, so the tiresome thing is read backwards

parts.note: a drag is a bore, a tiresome thing

explanation.surface: Someone close to a toppled glass muses that it was a tiresome business, looking back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'near' is old slang for mean with money, so 'I'm near' is the miser describing himself; the definition is a self-description standing for the person.
explanation.definitionFit: A miserly person is close-fisted, which is the old sense of near: tight with money.

clue.text: Drunk has pint around back of dive — Guinness maybe

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go around the last letter of dive
drunk means reeling and disordered, so these letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter, here of dive

explanation.surface: A drunk downs a pint of Guinness in the back of a seedy bar.
explanation.walkthrough: Guinness looks like the stout; it is the actor Sir Alec Guinness. HAS PINT rearranged ('Drunk') goes 'around' E, the 'back of' dive.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Alec Guinness was a celebrated stage and film actor, an example of a performer of drama.

clue.text: View oddly taken in working part of range?

indicators.note: taken in means held inside, so the picked letters go within the word for working

parts.note: a machine that is on is working

indicators.note: oddly picks the odd-numbered letters, first and third, of view

explanation.surface: A sight glimpsed strangely while working on part of a mountain range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'range' is a kitchen stove, not a line of mountains.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchen range is a cooking stove combining hob and baking compartment, so the baking chamber is one part.

clue.text: Foreman's aim, maybe, that's excellent?

definitions.meaning: George Foreman, the heavyweight boxer, aimed to floor opponents for the count
something stunning or terrific, a real stunner

explanation.surface: A work supervisor's target, perhaps, is something outstanding.
explanation.walkthrough: Foreman is not a works supervisor but George Foreman, the American heavyweight boxing champion.
explanation.definitionFit: A boxer seeks a win by flooring the opponent; informally the same word names something stunningly good.

clue.text: Group on board beset by rest finally dismissed as extremely eccentric

indicators.note: beset by means surrounded by, so the group goes inside the shortened rest
the final letter of the word for rest is sent away

parts.note: a siesta is an afternoon rest
a crew is the group working aboard a ship

explanation.surface: A ship's company surrounded by others, finally sent off for being thoroughly odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally dismissed' leaves SIEST, which 'beset by' wraps round the group.
explanation.definitionFit: Screwy is slang for crazy or odd, and the superlative form means the most eccentric of all.

clue.text: Cheer supported by woman, your uppity boisterous type

indicators.note: in a down light, the cheer sits on top of what follows, which supports it

parts.note: hooray is a shout of cheer
hen is slang for a woman, especially in Scotland

indicators.note: uppity reads as going up, so in this down light the abbreviation is read bottom to top

explanation.surface: A cheer backed by a woman, your typical haughty rowdy.
explanation.walkthrough: A Hooray Henry is a British term for a loud, upper-class young man.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a brash, rowdy young toff, a boisterous upper-class type.

clue.text: It might be consumed in Tijuana chow?

definitions.text: It might be consumed in Tijuana chow?

indicators.note: in signals that the letters sit inside the words Tijuana chow, straddling the gap

explanation.surface: A Mexican snack is something you might eat in Tijuana.
explanation.definitionFit: A tortilla chip topped with cheese is a classic Mexican snack, food eaten in a border city like Tijuana.

clue.text: Earmark space for fighting criminal

parts.note: a boxing ring is the space where fighters meet
a fence is a criminal who handles stolen goods

explanation.surface: Set aside an arena for a crook to brawl in.
explanation.definitionFit: To earmark funds is to reserve them for one purpose, protecting them as if behind a barrier.

clue.text: Approach around London college that's far from conventional?

indicators.note: around means the word for approach goes round the college abbreviation

parts.note: to near something is to approach it
UCL is University College London

explanation.surface: Getting close to a London university that is anything but traditional.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conventional' is the military sense: weapons that are not atomic.
explanation.definitionFit: Atomic weapons are the opposite of conventional arms in military terms, so atomic is far from conventional.

clue.text: Gave a summary description of long-time international footballer?

definitions.meaning: went over the main points again, summarised
a player selected for his country again and again has been awarded caps repeatedly

explanation.surface: A commentator summarised the career of a veteran international footballer.
explanation.walkthrough: A player picked for his national team is said to win a cap, so one capped again is re-capped.
explanation.definitionFit: To summarise is to restate the main points briefly; also a pun on a player capped again.

clue.text: Protest about battle site attended by Republican in leaderless country

indicators.note: attended by means accompanied, so what follows comes next

parts.note: re means about or concerning
Mons in Belgium was the site of First World War battles

indicators.note: in places the Republican letter inside the shortened country
leaderless means the first letter is removed

parts.note: a state is a country

explanation.surface: Objecting to a battlefield accompanied by a Republican in a country without a leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaderless' turns STATE into TATE; R goes 'in' to make TRATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To protest is to object forcefully, to argue against something.

clue.text: Inspector transported into Kent in row

parts.note: DI is a Detective Inspector

indicators.note: into means the second word goes inside the abbreviation for Kent

parts.note: Kent is a county in South East England, abbreviated SE
put means placed or moved somewhere

explanation.surface: A police inspector shipped into Kent in the middle of a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent, a county in south-east England, stands for SE, its compass region.
explanation.definitionFit: A row is a quarrel or argument, the sense rhyming with cow.

clue.text: International financier getting clipped, one facing New York in disgrace

indicators.note: clipped means cut short, so the last letter goes

parts.note: the gnomes of Zurich are Swiss bankers, so a gnome is a financier
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A global financier, cut down to size and facing New York, ends in shame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gnomes of Zurich' is a nickname for Swiss bankers; 'clipped' trims GNOME to GNOM.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignominy is public shame or dishonour, a synonym for disgrace.

clue.text: Poetic heroine embraced by warm audience

indicators.note: embraced by means held within, so the name lies inside the words warm audience

explanation.surface: A poem's heroine receives a warm welcome from the audience.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennyson's poem of that name addresses its heroine in the line 'Come into the garden'.

clue.text: Unstable pound dawned sadly after exposure of leading journalist

indicators.note: sadly means badly or wretchedly, so the letters are rearranged
exposure here means removal, putting out, so the journalist's letters are taken away

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder
ED, the editor, is the leading journalist on a paper

explanation.surface: Sterling wobbled when a dismal morning brought a top editor's scandal into the open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exposure' here means removal, not revelation; 'sadly' then rearranges the remaining POUNDDAWN.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that fluctuates, rising and falling, is erratic and unsteady.

clue.text: One once waiting endlessly during TV for item of news?

indicators.note: during means the second part goes inside the word for TV

parts.note: a TV is a set

indicators.note: endlessly means the final letter is removed

parts.note: a Nippy was a waitress in Lyons tea shops of the past

explanation.surface: An old-time waitress, waiting without end on the TV for a news item.
explanation.walkthrough: Nippies were waitresses in J. Lyons tea shops in Britain until the 1960s; 'endlessly' cuts NIPPY to NIPP.
explanation.definitionFit: A short extract or scrap of information, like a brief news morsel, is a fragment.

clue.text: Second source of catering in cooking house attracting following?

definitions.text: Second source of catering in cooking house attracting following?

indicators.note: attracting means drawing in something extra, so the following letter is added on
in places the catering letter inside the scrambled house
cooking as in cooking the books means fiddling, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

indicators.note: the source of a word is its first letter, here of catering

explanation.surface: A deputy chef is the second person cooking in a house, with followers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooking' rearranges HOUSE, with C ('source of catering') 'in' it, giving OUSCHE.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchen's second-in-command, deputy to the head cook, runs the catering under him.

clue.text: Woman that's first bound to hide new cover for note

indicators.note: to hide means to hold inside, so the new letter is concealed in the woman

parts.note: Eve was the first woman in Genesis
to lope is to run with long bounding strides

explanation.surface: The first woman, bound to keep news hidden, covers up a note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bound' is not obliged but a leaping stride.
explanation.definitionFit: A letter or note is posted in a paper wrapper sealed around it.

clue.text: Long time needed to take in tons in Berkshire town

indicators.note: to take in means to contain, so the tons letter goes inside

parts.note: an eon is an immensely long time

explanation.surface: It takes ages to take in tonnes of stuff in a Berkshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Berkshire is an English county west of London; the town is home to the famous school.
explanation.definitionFit: The town is in Berkshire, England, across the Thames from Windsor and famed for its college.

clue.text: Delightful place? See one in total

parts.note: Ely is a cathedral city, a bishop's see

indicators.note: in means the one goes inside the word for total

parts.note: a sum is a total
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Visit someone in full, as one goes to a lovely spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is not look but a bishop's see, or diocese: Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the paradise of the blessed dead is a place of perfect happiness.

clue.text: Turn buns in barbecue getting very red?

indicators.note: a barbecue grills and chars things, so the letters are thrown about and remade

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Flip the buns on the barbecue as they start to char.
explanation.definitionFit: Skin burned by too much sunshine turns red, the reddening of a sunbather.

clue.text: Common illness fellow avoided starts to die away in couple of years

indicators.note: avoided means left out, so the fellow letter goes

parts.note: a fever is an illness

indicators.note: in places the first letters inside the two years

parts.note: Y is the abbreviation for year, so two of them give YY

indicators.note: the starts are the first letters of die and away

explanation.surface: A common bug, its sufferer escaping, starts to fade away within a couple of years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'avoided' drops F from FEVER to give EVER; DA, the starts of die away, goes 'in' YY.
explanation.definitionFit: Something common is ordinary or routine, as things are that happen daily.

clue.text: Island lacking money and rule, site of worship?

indicators.note: lacking means without, so the money letter is dropped

parts.note: Malta is a Mediterranean island

explanation.surface: A poor island with no laws: where do the people go to worship?
explanation.definitionFit: In church, the communion table stands at the focus of worship and offering.

clue.text: Nerve perhaps encapsulating Conservative advocate of reform

indicators.note: encapsulating means enclosing, so the Conservative letter goes inside

parts.note: the radial nerve runs down the arm, an example of a nerve

explanation.surface: A man's nerve wraps a Tory into the camp of reformers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nerve' looks like courage; it is an arm nerve.
explanation.definitionFit: A person seeking sweeping political change from the roots up is a reformer.

clue.text: Bachelor abandoning premier hideout

indicators.note: abandoning means leaving, so the bachelor letter departs

parts.note: Tony Blair was British prime minister, a premier

explanation.surface: A single man leaves the Prime Minister's secret retreat.
explanation.walkthrough: Tony Blair was the UK prime minister at the time of this puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild animal's den is its hiding place, and figuratively any hideaway.

clue.text: Partner getting a meat dish skirting two islands in retreat

indicators.note: skirting means going around the edge, so the dish surrounds the islands

parts.note: saté, also satay, is skewered grilled meat

indicators.note: retreating means going backwards, so the islands read in reverse

parts.note: I is an abbreviation for island, and Cos is a Greek island
Cos is an island in the Greek Dodecanese

explanation.surface: A partner takes a meat dish round a pair of islands on a getaway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in retreat' gives SOCI; Cos is a Greek island and saté a skewered-meat dish.
explanation.definitionFit: A partner in business is a colleague or co-worker sharing in an enterprise.

clue.text: Item of punishment releasing sweat

indicators.note: releasing means setting free, so the letters are let loose into a new order

explanation.surface: A beating that sets off a cold sweat.
explanation.walkthrough: A tawse is a leather strap formerly used in Scottish schools to punish pupils.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish leather strap used to hit pupils' hands was an instrument of school discipline.

clue.text: Besides Troy, bust is found amid wild excitement

indicators.note: is found amid means sits in the middle of, so the pieces go inside

parts.note: a furore is an uproar of wild excitement
T is an abbreviation for troy, the system of weights
a herm is a bust of Hermes on a square pillar

explanation.surface: Next to Troy, a statue is discovered amid frenzied excitement.
explanation.walkthrough: Troy is not the city but the troy weight system, abbreviated T; a herm is a bust on a pillar.
explanation.definitionFit: Besides, used to add a further point, means in addition or moreover.
